# Independent Set Hardness in Graphs of Bounded Twin-Width and Low-Radius Merge-Width

**Édouard Bonnet** \(\unknown\) **Univers Lyon, CNRS, ENS de Lyon, Université Claude Bernard Lyon 1, LIP UMR5668, France**

**Maël Dumas** \(\unknown\) **Institute of Informatics, University of Warsaw, Poland**

**Julien Duron** \(\unknown\) **Institute of Informatics, University of Warsaw, Poland**

**Abstract**

For every \(\varepsilon>0\), Max Independent Set admits a polynomial-time \(n^\varepsilon\)-approximation algorithm on _n_-vertex graphs of effectively bounded twin-width [Bergé et al., STACS ’23]. The approximation factor actually obtained is more precisely _n_<sup>O(1/loglog_n_)</sup>. Prior to the current paper, no approximation hardness was known for this problem, and the existence of a polynomial-time approximation scheme (PTAS) was repeatedly raised as an open question. We answer this question in a strong sense: We show that there is a constant \(\gamma>0\) such that a polynomial-time \(n^{\gamma/(loglogn)^2}\)-approximation algorithm for Max Independent Set on graphs of twin-width at most 4 would refute the Exponential-Time Hypothesis (ETH). This lower bound further holds if a 4-sequence is provided as part of the input. We show the same hardness of approximation for Min Coloring, which also has a nearly matching _n_<sup>O(1/loglog_n_)</sup>-approximation algorithm on graphs of effectively bounded twin-width.

We also clarify the parameterized complexity of _k_-Independent Set on graphs of bounded radius-_r_ merge-width when the range of _r_ is limited. There is a fixed-parameter tractable algorithm for _k_-Independent Set on graphs given with radius-2<sup>O(_k_<sup>2</sup>)</sup> merge sequences of bounded width [Dreier and Toruńczyk, S ’25]. We complement this result by showing that _k_-Independent Set is W[1]-hard on graphs given with radius-_o(k_) merge sequences of bounded width. We further show that this result also holds for _k_-Dominating Set.

### 1 Introduction

The problem of finding in a graph a largest subset of pairwise non-adjacent vertices, Max Independent Set (MIS for short), is NP-complete [20], and very hard to approximate: For any \(\varepsilon>0\), an \(n^{1-\varepsilon}\)-approximation algorithm would imply that P=NP [22, 26]. The best known polynomial-time approximation factor is \(\frac{n(loglogn)^2}{log^3n}\) [18]. In contrast, this central problem enjoys much better approximation algorithms on structured graph classes. A historical example is that of planar graphs where, due to Baker’s shifting technique, a polynomial-time approximation scheme (PTAS) exists [2]. MIS also has a PTAS on minor-free classes [21] and on disk graphs [12]. If a geometric representation is provided, there is, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), an \(n^\varepsilon\)-approximation algorithm for the independence number of the intersection graph of _n_ curves every two of which have at most a constant number of intersections [19], and a quasipolynomial-time approximation scheme (QPTAS) for general string graphs [1].

In this paper, our focus is on classes of bounded twin-width [11] and of bounded merge- width [17]. These graph parameters were introduced in 2020 and 2025, respectively. Classes of bounded twin-width include classes of bounded clique-width, classes excluding a fixed minor, unit interval graphs, and _d_-dimensional grids [11]. Classes of bounded merge-width are even more general and further include classes of bounded expansion [17]. The main algorithmic application of classes of bounded twin-width and of bounded merge-width, when bounded-width witnesses are given, is that first-order model checking is fixed-parameter tractable [11, 17].

As we detail in the next paragraph, some improved approximation algorithms exist on classes of bounded twin-width. In general, however, there is no precise understanding of the provably best algorithms achievable when twin-width or merge-width is bounded. This is reflected in large approximability gaps and the lack of tight lower bounds under the Exponential-Time Hypothesis (ETH). Our motivation is to fill those gaps.

In classes of effectively<sup>1</sup> bounded twin-width, \(n\varepsilon\)-approximation algorithms for MIS, Min Coloring, and other related problems were shown for every \(\varepsilon>0\) [4]. The proof in [4] reveals that the approximation factor for MIS is more specifically _n_<sup>_c/_loglog_n_</sup>, for some constant _c_. While it was known that Max Independent Set is NP-hard on graphs of bounded twin-width [11], even bounded by 4 [3] (also see [8] for the status of other graph problems on graphs of low twin-width), no conditional hardness of approximation was established on classes of bounded twin-width. Even a polynomial-time approximation scheme (PTAS) was not excluded. Indeed, the existence of a PTAS was raised several times [9, 10, 4, 14, 7]. It was nonetheless observed that any O(1)-approximation algorithm would imply the existence of a PTAS [10].

We rule this out under the ETH and show a much tighter hardness-of-approximation result that nearly matches the _n_<sup>_c/_loglog_n_</sup>-approximation algorithm.

\(\blacktriangleright\) **Theorem 1.** _Unless the ETH fails, there is a constant_ \(\gamma>0\) _such that Max Independent Set does not admit a polynomial-time_ \(n^{\gamma/(loglogn)^2}\)_-approximation algorithm on n-vertex graphs of twin-width at most 4, even when a 4-sequence is given as part of the input._

The reduction uses, in order, three ingredients: (1) a classical reduction from 3-SAT to MIS, (2) a long even subdivision of the resulting instances, and (3) a lexicographic power of the resulting graphs.

"Long" subdivisions have twin-width at most 4 [3], which explains the role of (2). _Even_ subdivisions preserve the NP-hardness of MIS [25]. However, "long" subdivisions do not preserve any hardness of approximation. There is a straightforward PTAS on these graphs: select every other vertex along each subdivided edge. So, there is a psychological barrier in using (2). Nevertheless, with the right exponent, (3) resurrects this seemingly defunct approximation gap, while keeping the reduction within the desired running-time budget.

Similar ingredients can be adapted to give the same result for Min Coloring.

\(\blacktriangleright\) **Theorem 2 (** \(\includegraphics{}\)**).** _Unless the ETH fails, there is a constant_ \(\gamma>0\) _such that Min Coloring does not admit a polynomial-time_ \(n^{\gamma/(loglogn)^2}\)_-approximation algorithm on n-vertex graphs of twin-width at most 4, even when a 4-sequence is given as part of the input._

Theorem 2 implies Theorem 1. Indeed, a polynomial-time _r_-approximation algorithm for MIS implies a polynomial-time O(_r_log_n_)-approximation algorithm for Min Coloring. Repeatedly removing an _r_-approximate maximum independent set and assigning it a new

We keep both proofs because the proof of Theorem 1 implements the above outline without the extra technicalities needed for Min Coloring.

We then delineate the tractability boundary of _k_-Independent Set (_k_-IS for short) on graphs of bounded merge-width. Strictly speaking, merge-width is a _family_ of parameters. For every positive integer _r_, the radius-_r_ merge-width, denoted by mw<sub>_r_</sub>, must be bounded by a function of _r_, for the merge-width itself to be bounded. Low-radius merge-width, think mw<sub>1</sub>, mw<sub>2</sub>, or mw<sub>_c_</sub> for some constant _c_, is of independent interest. There are some properties that only require these parameters to be bounded. Notably, classes of bounded merge-width were proven \(\chi\)-bounded by showing the stronger statement that classes of bounded mw<sub>2</sub> are \(\chi\)-bounded [6] (and the \(\chi\)-boundedness of classes of bounded mw<sub>1</sub> remains open).

Given radius-2<sup>_ck_<sup>2</sup></sup> merge sequences of bounded width<sup>2</sup> for some appropriate constant _c\>_0, _k_-IS admits a fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) algorithm [17]. In fact, this is more generally the case for first-order model checking. Dreier and Toruńczyk ask whether a simpler and faster algorithm could exist for _k_-Independent Set (and _k_-Dominating Set).

A related question is whether these problems admit FPT algorithms given radius-_r_ merge sequences of bounded width already in the regime _r_=O(1). We rule this out for any radius _r=o(k_), with a reduction from the W[1]-hard Grid Tiling problem [24] to _k_-IS. We ensure that the produced graphs have bounded radius-_r_ merge-width by spacing the Grid Tiling cells out with "paths of co-matchings" of length \(\Theta(r)\).

\(\blacktriangleright\) **Theorem 3.** \(\forall r=o(k)\)_, k-Independent Set is W[1]-hard in graphs of bounded mw<sub>r</sub>._

We then adapt the previous reduction to get the same statement for _k_-Dominating Set.

\(\blacktriangleright\) **Theorem 4.** \(\forall r=o(k)\)_, k-Dominating Set is W[1]-hard in graphs of bounded mw<sub>r</sub>._

**Future work.** Our work naturally leads to the following questions. Combining Theorems 1 and 2 and [4], we now know that, unless the ETH fails, the best approximation factor for Max Independent Set and Min Coloring lies somewhere between \(n^{\Theta(1)/(loglogn)^2}\) and \(n^{\Theta(1)/loglogn}\). Can one obtain matching bounds, up to constants in the exponent?

Ruling out a PTAS for MIS on graphs of bounded twin-width under the weaker assumption that \(\mathrm{P}\neq\mathrm{NP}\) remains open. Let us also mention the question of obtaining nontrivial approximation algorithms for these problems when the contraction sequence is _not_ provided.

Theorems 3 and 4 and [17] raise the question of the smallest radius _r(k_) such that _k_-Independent Set (and _k_-Dominating Set) is FPT on graphs given with a radius-_r(k_) merge sequence of bounded width. We now know that this radius is between \(\Omega(k)\) and 2<sup>O(_k_<sup>2</sup>)</sup>.

## 2 Preliminaries

For two integers _i_ and _j_, we denote by [_i,j_] the set of integers that are at least _i_ and at most _j_. For every integer _i_, [_i_] is a shorthand for [1_,i_]. In this paper, the log function is in base 2.

The Exponential-Time Hypothesis (ETH) asserts that there is a real constant \(\lambda>1\) such that _n_-variable 3-SAT cannot be solved in time \(\mathcal{O}(\lambda^n)\).

### 2.1 Standard graph-theoretic definitions and notation

We denote by _V(G_) and _E(G_) the set of vertices and edges of a graph _G_, respectively. We denote by \(\|G\|\) the total size of _G_, that is, |_V(G_)|+|_E(G_)|. For \(S\subseteq V(G)\), the _subgraph of G induced by S_, denoted _G[S_], is obtained by removing from _G_ all the vertices that are not in _S_. We denote by _N<sub>G</sub>(v_) the set of neighbors of _v_ in _G_. We denote by dist_<sub>G</sub>(u,v_) the length of a shortest path between _u_ and _v_ in _G_, and set \(\mathrm{Ball}_G^r(v):=\{w\in V(G)|\mathrm{dist}_G(v,w)\le r\}\).

A _subdivision_ of a graph _G_ is any graph _H_ obtained from _G_ by replacing edges _e_ of _G_ by paths with at least one edge whose extremities are the endpoints of _e_. A \((\ge s)\)_-subdivision_ is a subdivision where every edge is replaced by a path with at least _s_ internal vertices.

### 2.2 Trigraphs, contraction sequences, and twin-width

A _trigraph G_ has vertex set _V(G_), black edge set _E(G_), red edge set _R(G_) such that \(E(G)\cap R(G)=\emptyset\) (and \(E(G),R(G)\subseteq\left(V(G)2\right)\)). Two vertices _u,v_ such that \(uv\in R(G)\) are called _red neighbors_. The _red degree_ of _u_ is its number of red neighbors. The _maximum red degree_ of _G_ is the maximum red degree among all its vertices.

For distinct vertices \(u,v\in V(G)\), the _contraction_ of _u_ and _v_ replaces them with a new vertex _w_. For every \(x\in V(G)\backslash\{u,v\}\), the pair _wx_ is a black edge if both _ux_ and _vx_ are black edges, it is a non-edge if both _ux_ and _vx_ are non-edges, and it is a red edge otherwise. All pairs not incident with _u_ or _v_ remain unchanged.

A _contraction sequence_ of a graph _G_, viewed as a trigraph with no red edges, is a sequence _G=G<sub>n</sub>,G_<sub>_n_-1</sub>_,...,G_<sub>1</sub> such that |_V(G<sub>i</sub>_)|=_i_ and _G_<sub>_i_-1</sub> is obtained from _G<sub>i</sub>_ by contracting two vertices. The sequence is a _d-sequence_ if, for every \(i\in[n]\), the trigraph _G<sub>i</sub>_ has maximum red degree at most _d_. The _twin-width_ of _G_, denoted by tww(_G_), is the minimum integer _d_ for which _G_ admits a _d_-sequence.

To show Theorems 1 and 2, we will rely on the fact that long-enough subdivisions of general graphs have bounded twin-width.

\(\blacktriangleright\) **Lemma 5** (Theorem 7 in [3])**.** _For every n-vertex graph G, the_ \(2\lceil\mathrm{log}n\rceil\)_-subdivision H of G has twin-width at most 4. Furthermore, a 4-sequence of H can be computed in_ \(\mathcal{O}(\|H\|)\) _time._

The algorithmic statement of Lemma 5 is implicit in [3] and follows from the proof.

We say that a graph class C has _effectively bounded twin-width_ if there is a polynomial-time algorithm A and a fixed integer _d_ such that on every graph \(G\in\mathcal{C}\), A outputs a _d_-sequence of _G_. We observe that most classes currently known to have bounded twin-width have effectively bounded twin-width.

## 2.3 Merge-width

For two sets _X,Y_ , we write \(XY:=\{xy|x\in X,y\in Y,x\neq y\}\), where _xy_ denotes the unordered pair {_x,y_}. Let P be a partition of the vertices _V_ of a graph _G_. For a set \(X\subseteq V\) , we denote by _X/_P the set of parts of P intersecting _X_. Let \(R\subseteq\genfrac(){pt}{2}{V}{2}\) be a set of pairs of vertices of _G_. The distance between _x_ and _y_ in (_V,R_) is denoted by dist_<sub>R</sub>(x,y_), and we define \(\mathrm{Ball}_R^r(x):=\{y\in V|\mathrm{dist}_R(x,y)\le r\}\). The _radius-r width_ of (P_,R_) is defined as

\(max_{v\in V}|\mathrm{Ball}_R^r(v)/\mathcal{P}|.\)

We say that P is _homogeneous modulo R_ (in _G_) if for any parts \(X,Y\in\mathcal{P}\) (possibly _X=Y_ ) and pairs \(xy,x'y'\in XY\backslash R\), we have that \(xy\in E(G)\) if and only if \(x'y'\in E(G)\). A partition P is _coarser_ than a partition \(\mathcal{P}'\), denoted by \(\mathcal{P}'\unknown\mathcal{P}\), if every part of \(\mathcal{P}'\) is contained in a part of P.

\(\blacktriangleright\) **Definition 6** (Definition 3.1 in [17])**.** _A_ merge sequence _for a graph G is a sequence_ (P<sub>1</sub>_,R_<sub>1</sub>)_,...,_(P_<sub>m</sub>,R<sub>m</sub>_) _such that:_

\(\mathbf{1}.\mathcal{P}_1\unknown\mathcal{P}_2\unknown\dots\unknown\mathcal{P}_m\text{\textit{is a sequence of ever coarser partitions of}}V(G)\text{\textit{, with}}\mathcal{P}_1\text{\textit{the
partition into singletons and}}\mathcal{P}_m\text{\textit{the partition with one part,}}\)

\(\mathbf{2}.R_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq R_m\subseteq\genfrac(){pt}{2}{V(G)}{2}\text{\textit{is a monotone sequence of sets of pairs of vertices, and}}\)

\(\mathbf{3}.\mathcal{P}_t\text{\textit{is homogeneous modulo}}R_t\text{\textit{, for}}t=1,\dots,m\text{\textit{.}}\)

_The_ radius-_r_ width _of this merge sequence is the maximum radius-r width of_ (P_<sub>t</sub>,R_<sub>_t_+1</sub>)_, for_ \(1\le t<m\)_. Finally, the_ radius-_r_ merge-width _of G, denoted by mw<sub>r</sub>(G), is the minimum radius-r width of a merge sequence for G._

The elements of _R<sub>t</sub>_ are called _resolved pairs_ (at step _t_). Note that the partition P<sub>_t_+1</sub> is obtained by merging some parts of P_<sub>t</sub>_. Note also that the index mismatch in (P_<sub>t</sub>,R_<sub>_t_+1</sub>) is intentional, and prevents one from merging many parts and adding many resolved pairs all at once when going from step _t_ to _t_+1.

A graph class C has _bounded merge-width_ if there is a function _f_ such that for every \(G\in\mathcal{C}\) and every positive integer _r_, we have \(\mathrm{mw}_r(G)\le f(r)\).

**Organization.** We prove Theorem 1 in Section 3, Theorem 2 in Section 4, Theorem 3 in Section 5, and Theorem 4 in Section 6.

## 3 Approximation Hardness of MIS in Graphs of Bounded Twin-Width

In this paper, all 3-SAT instances have only 3-clauses. Equal literals within the same clause are allowed, but we disallow opposite literals of the same variable within the same clause. A 3-SAT-_B_ formula has no variable occurring (positively or negatively) more than _B_ times. The following theorem is a consequence of Dinur’s almost-linear PCP [15] and some folklore reductions; see, for instance, [23, Thm. 7].

\(\blacktriangleright\) **Theorem 7** (consequence of Theorem 8.3 in [15])**.** _Unless the ETH fails, there are positive constants_ \(\beta<1,B,c\) _such that distinguishing n-variable m-clause 3-SAT-B satisfiable formulas from instances where at most_ \(\beta m\) _clauses can be satisfied requires_ \(2^{\Omega(n/\mathrm{log}^cn)}\) _time._

We denote by \(e(\varphi)\) the total number of unordered pairs of opposing literals appearing in \(\varphi\). For instance, if \(\varphi=x_1\vee\neg x_2\vee x_4,\neg x_1\vee\neg x_1\vee x_2,\neg x_2\vee x_3\vee\neg x_4\), we have \(e(\varphi)=2+2+0+1=5\). We denote by \(\mathrm{val}(\varphi)\) the largest number of clauses satisfied by any truth assignment. In particular, if \(\varphi\) is satisfiable, then \(\mathrm{val}(\varphi)\) is equal to its number of clauses.

\(\blacktriangleright\) **Theorem 8.** _There is an_ \(\mathcal{O}((m+e(\varphi))logm)\)_-time algorithm that, given an m-clause 3-SAT formula_ \(\varphi\)_, outputs a graph_ \(G_\varphi\) _of twin-width at most 4 such that_ \(|V(G_\varphi)|=3m+(e(\varphi)+3m)\cdot 2\lceil log(3m)\rceil\)_, and_ \(\alpha(G_\varphi)=val(\varphi)+(e(\varphi)+3m)\cdot\lceil log(3m)\rceil\). _Furthermore, a 4-sequence of_ \(G_\varphi\) _can be computed in_ \(\mathcal{O}(\|G_\varphi\|)\) _time._ **Proof.** Let \(J_\varphi\) be the graph with one vertex per literal occurrence in a clause of \(\varphi\), and an edge between every two literals that are either in the same clause or that are of the same variable with opposite signs. In particular, \(J_\varphi\) has exactly 3_m_ vertices and exactly \(3m+e(\varphi)\) edges (recall our definition of 3-SAT). Then, \(G_\varphi\) is the _s_-subdivision of \(J_\varphi\) with \(s:=2\lceil log(3m)\rceil\). Note that \(G_\varphi\) can be built from \(\varphi\) in \(\mathcal{O}((m+e(\varphi))logm)\) time. By Lemma 5, \(G_\varphi\) has twin-width at most 4, and a 4-sequence of \(G_\varphi\) can be computed in \(\mathcal{O}(\|G_\varphi\|)\) time. Since \(G_\varphi\) is a _s_-subdivision of a 3_m_-vertex \((3m+e(\varphi))\)-edge graph, \(|V(G_\varphi)|=3m+(e(\varphi)+3m)\cdot s\). The second item dates back to Poljak [25]. We sketch this classic fact. The inequality \(\alpha(G_\varphi)\ge val(\varphi)+(e(\varphi)+3m)\cdot\frac{s}{2}\) holds, as there is an independent set of \(G_\varphi\) with one vertex corresponding to a satisfied literal for each clause satisfied by a fixed truth assignment that satisfies \(val(\varphi)\) clauses of \(\varphi\), and \(\frac{s}{2}\) vertices per subdivided edge of \(J_\varphi\). The inequality \(\alpha(G_\varphi)\le val(\varphi)+(e(\varphi)+3m)\cdot\frac{s}{2}\) holds since a larger independent set of \(G_\varphi\) would contain more than \(val(\varphi)\) original vertices (those of \(J_\varphi\)). This would imply that \(J_\varphi\) has an independent set of size greater than \(val(\varphi)\). (We elaborate on this in the proof of Theorem 13.) The (consistent, partial) truth assignment setting the corresponding literals to true would contradict the definition of \(val(\varphi)\). \(\blacktriangleleft\) Given a graph _G_ and a positive integer _k_, we denote by _G_[_k_] the _k-th lexicographic power_ of _G_ with _V(G_[_k_])=_V(G)k_ and \((u_1,\dots,u_k)(v_1,\dots,v_k)\in E(G^{[k]})\) whenever there is some \(i\in[k]\) such that \(u_iv_i\in E(G)\) and for every \(h\in[i-1]\), _uh=vh_. The following is a folklore observation. We give a recent reference for completeness. \(\blacktriangleright\) **Lemma 9** (see Lemma 7.12 in [10])**.** _For every graph G and integer_ \(k\ge 1\), \(\alpha(G^{[k]})=\alpha(G)^k\). _Furthermore, there is an algorithm that, given an independent set S of G_[_k_]_, outputs an independent set of G of size at least_ |_S_|1_/k_ _in_ \(\mathcal{O}(\|G^{[k]}\|)\) _time._ The twin-width of every lexicographic power of a graph _G_ is equal to that of _G_. \(\blacktriangleright\) **Lemma 10** (Lemma 7.11 in [10])**.** _For every graph G and integer_ \(k\ge 1\)_, tww(G_[_k_])=_tww(G)._ _Furthermore, given a d-sequence of G, one can compute a d-sequence of G_[_k_] _in time_ O(|_V(G_[_k_])|). We now have all the ingredients to show our main result, which we restate for convenience. \(\blacktriangleright\) **Theorem 1.** _Unless the ETH fails, there is a constant_ \(\gamma>0\) _such that Max Independent Set does not admit a polynomial-time_ \(n^{\gamma/(loglogn)^2}\)_-approximation algorithm on n-vertex graphs of twin-width at most 4, even when 4-sequences are given as part of the input._ **Proof.** Fix the constants \(\beta<1,B,c\) so as to satisfy Theorem 7. We make the following reduction. Every _N_-variable _m_-clause 3-SAT-_B_ formula \(\varphi\) is mapped to the graph \(H:=G_\varphi^{[k]}\) with \(k:=\lceil m/log^{c+2}m\rceil\). We will assume that _m_ is large enough. In particular, the following inequalities hold: \(\text{1.}log\left(4(3B^2+6)log(3m)\right) \(\text{2.}logm>2loglog^{c+2}m+log3;\)

## 3. \(\frac{(e(\varphi)+3m)\cdot\lceil log(3m)\rceil}{(1-\beta)m}>2\).

Building _H_ takes O(_m_log_m_)+(_m_log_m_)<sup>O(_k_)</sup> time. Indeed, note that \(e(\varphi)\le B^2N\le 3B^2m\). So the first term in the running time corresponds to building \(G_\varphi\), and the second term, to building its _k_-th lexicographic power _H_. By Theorem 8 and Lemma 10, _H_ indeed has twin-width at most 4, and a 4-sequence of _H_ can be computed in time polynomial in \(\|H\|\).

Suppose there is an _n_<sup>O(1)</sup>-time _r_-approximation algorithm A for Max Independent Set on _n_-vertex graphs of twin-width at most 4. Our proof will work even if A has access to a 4-sequence of _H_.

Let \(\delta\le\Delta:=6(B^2+1)\) be such that

\((e(\varphi)+3m)\cdot\lceil log(3m)\rceil=\delta mlog(3m).\)

We set the constant

\(\gamma:=\frac{0.8(1-\beta)}{8(\beta+\Delta)}.\)

To conclude the proof, we assume that \(r=n^{\gamma/(loglogn)^2}\) with \(n:=|V(G_\varphi)|^k\), and proceed to refute the ETH.

When run on _H_, A returns an independent set _I<sub>H</sub>_ of _H_ of size at least \(\alpha(H)/r\). By Lemma 9, we find in time O((_m_log_m_)<sup>2_k_</sup>) an independent set _I_ of \(G_\varphi\) of size at least

\(\left(\frac{\alpha(H)}{r}\right)^{1/k}=\frac{\alpha(G_\varphi)}{r^{1/k}}.\)

We report that \(\varphi\) is satisfiable if \(|I|>\beta m+\delta mlog(3m)\), and that at most \(\beta m\) clauses of \(\varphi\) are satisfiable, otherwise.

**Running time.** Let us first verify that the overall process takes 2<sup>_o(N/_log<sup>_c_</sup>_N_)</sup>. Building _H_, optionally computing a 4-sequence of _H_, running A on _H_, finding _I_, and concluding whether \(\varphi\) is satisfiable takes time

\((mlogm)^{\mathcal{O}(k)}+n^{\mathcal{O}(1)}+\mathcal{O}((mlogm)^{2k})=m^{\mathcal{O}(m/log^{c+2}m)}=2^{\mathcal{O}(m/log^{c+1}m)}\)

and, since \(m\le BN\) and \(m\ge N/3\),

\(2^{\mathcal{O}(m/log^{c+1}m)}=2^{\mathcal{O}(BN/log^{c+1}(N/3))}=2^{o(N/log^cN)}.\)

**Correctness.** We now check that we are correct on the satisfiability of \(\varphi\), and thus conclude by Theorem 7. The crux of the argument is the following claim.

\(\vartriangleright\) Claim 11. \((m+\delta mlog(3m))\cdot\frac{1}{r^{1/k}}>\beta m+\delta mlog(3m)\).

Proof. We first recall that

\(n=|V(G_\varphi)|^k=(3m+(e(\varphi)+3m)\cdot 2\lceil log(3m)\rceil)^k\le\left(4(3B^2+6)mlog(3m)\right)^k.\)

So,

\(logn\le klogm+klog\left(4(3B^2+6)log(3m)\right)<2klog(3m),\) (1)

where the last inequality holds by Item 1. And

\(loglogn\ge logk\ge logm-loglog^{c+2}m>\frac{1}{2}log(3m),\)

Finally, for (P<sub>3</sub>_,F_<sub>4</sub>), the edges of _G_ are only between consecutive blocks inside a cell gadget, or between adjacent border blocks. Since any block of _G_ is in one part of P<sub>3</sub>, for any \(v\in V(G)\), we have \(|\mathrm{Ball}_{F_4}^{r-1}(v)/\mathcal{P}_3|\le 4r-3\). This concludes the proof.

These claims readily give that _k_-IS is W[1]-hard on graphs of bounded radius-_r_ merge- width, where _r_ is a fixed constant. However, we can extract more. Fix two computable functions _f(x_)=_o(x_) and \(g(x)\ge 4x\). Then we say that _G_ has (_f,g,k)-merge-width_ if \(\mathrm{mw}_{f(k)}(G)\le g(k)\).

\(\vartriangleright\) Claim 17. _k_-Independent Set on graphs with (_f,g,k_)-merge-width is W[1]-hard.

Proof. We design an FPT reduction from Grid Tiling with parameter _q_ to _k_-Independent Set with _k_:=(2_r_-1)_q_<sup>2</sup>, where _r_:=_r(q_) is the smallest odd integer at least equal to 3 such that

\(f((2r-1)q^2)\le r-1.\)

This integer exists since _f(x_)=_o(x_), and is computable since _f_ is computable.

Let (S_,q,n_) be an instance of Grid Tiling. Computing \(G:=G_\mathcal{S}^r\) can be done in time \(\mathcal{O}(\|G\|)=\mathcal{O}(r^2q^4\cdot n^4)\). This is an FPT reduction in parameter _q_ since _r_ depends only on _q_. Besides, _G_ has (_f,g,k_)-merge-width, since

\(\mathrm{mw}_{f(k)}(G)=\mathrm{mw}_{f((2r-1)q^2)}(G)\le\mathrm{mw}_{r-1}(G)\le 4r-3\le 4(2r-1)q^2\le g((2r-1)q^2)=g(k).\)

Where the first inequality comes from monotonicity of merge-width with respect to the radius, the second is due to Claim 16, and the last, by the assumption on _g_. We conclude by Claim 15.

In particular, for every _r=o(k_), _k_-IS is W[1]-hard on graphs of bounded mw_<sub>r</sub>_.

## 6 _k_-Dominating Set in graphs of bounded low-radius merge-width

In this section, we adapt the reduction from the previous section to show the W[1]-hardness of _k_-Dominating Set in graphs of low-radius merge-width. The main difference is how the selection of copies of the same tile in a cell gadget is enforced. First, instead of cliques, the blocks will be independent sets. Then, we will achieve the vertex selection by inserting between every pair of consecutive blocks _B_ and \(B'\), an additional block _A_ such that there is a co-matching between _B_ and _A_, and a matching between _A_ and \(B'\). The only way to dominate this new block _A_ with two vertices will be to pick copies of the same tile in _B_ and \(B'\). A similar construction can be done to enforce that selected tiles in adjacent cells agree on their corresponding component (see Figure 2).

\(\blacktriangleright\) **Theorem 4.** _k-Dominating Set is W[1]-hard in graphs of bounded mw_<sub>_o(k_)</sub>.

**Proof.** Let _r\>_3 be an odd integer, for a Grid Tiling instance (S_,k,n_) we will construct a graph \(G_\mathcal{S}^r\) with \(\mathrm{mw}_{2r-2}(G_\mathcal{S}^r)=\mathcal{O}(r)\). For each grid cell \(\pi\in[k]^2\), we construct a cell gadget \(C_\pi^r\). The cell gadget \(C_\pi^r\) consists of a horizontal path and a vertical path of 2_r_-1 edgeless graphs:

\(B_\pi^{h_1},B_\pi^{h_2},\dots,B_\pi^{h_{2r-1}}\) where \(B_\pi^{h_i}\) have vertex set \(\{b(\tau,h_i,\pi)|\tau\in S_\pi\}\); and

\(B_\pi^{v_1},B_\pi^{v_2},\dots,B_\pi^{v_{2r-1}}\) where \(B_\pi^{v_i}\) have vertex set \(\{b(\tau,v_i,\pi)|\tau\in S_\pi\}\). They are crossing in the middle, i.e., \(B_\pi^{h_r}=B_\pi^{v_r}\).

For every even block we add a co-matching towards the previous block and a matching towards the next block. That is, for \(\tau,\tau'\in S_\pi\) with \(\tau\neq\tau'\) and even \(i\in[2r-1]\), add to \(C_\pi^r\) edges between

\(b(\tau,h_i,\pi)\) and \(b(\tau',h_{i-1},\pi);b(\tau,h_i,\pi)\) and \(b(\tau,h_{i+1},\pi)\);

\(b(\tau,v_i,\pi)\) and \(b(\tau',v_{i-1},\pi);b(\tau,v_i,\pi)\) and \(b(\tau,v_{i+1},\pi)\).

Additionally, for each odd \(i\in[2r-1]\), add

vertices \(a_1(h_i,\pi)\) and \(a_2(h_i,\pi)\) complete to \(B_\pi^{h_i}\); and

vertices \(a_1(v_i,\pi)\) and \(a_2(v_i,\pi)\) complete to \(B_\pi^{v_i}\).

Note that since _r_ is odd, a pair of such vertices is created for \(B_\pi^{h_r}=B_\pi^{v_r}\). This is done to guarantee that a vertex is picked in each odd block. The endpoints of the paths are called _border blocks_, and any other block in \(C_\pi^r\) is called an _interior block_.

We construct \(G_\mathcal{S}^r\) by taking the disjoint union of all the \(C_\pi^r\) for \(\pi\in[k]^2\). Additionally, to ensure that the same first or second component is selected between adjacent gadget cells, we add the following vertices and edges.

For each \(\pi\in[k-1]\times[k]\), add a set of vertices \(\{r(i,\pi)|i\in[n]\}\) and edges between \(b((i,\text{\_}),h_{2r-1},\pi)\in B_\pi^{h_{2r-1}}\) and \(r(j,\pi)\) for \(i,j\in[n]\) with \(i\neq j\); and \(b((i,\text{\_}),h_1,\pi_\blacktriangleright)\in B_{\pi^\blacktriangleright}^{h_1}\) and \(r(i,\pi)\) for \(i\in[n]\).

For each \(\pi\in[k]\times[k-1]\), add a set of vertices \(\{d(i,\pi)|i\in[n]\}\) and edges between \(b((\text{\_},i),v_{2r-1},\pi)\in B_\pi^{v_{2r-1}}\) and \(d(j,\pi)\) for \(i\neq j\in[n]\); and \(b((\text{\_},i),v_1,\pi_\triangledown)\in B_{\pi_\triangledown}^{v_1}\) and \(d(i,\pi)\) for \(i\in[n]\).

This concludes the construction of \(G_\mathcal{S}^r\) and note that \(|V(G_\mathcal{S}^r)|=\mathcal{O}(rn^2k^2)\).

The following claims can be shown similarly to their counterparts in Theorem 3. For the equivalence of Grid Tiling and _k_-Dominating Set instances, it follows from the fact that the only dominating sets of size 2_r_-1 of a gadget cell \(C_\pi^r\) are of the form

\(Dom_\pi:=\{b(\tau,h_{2i-1},\pi),b(\tau,v_{2i-1},\pi)|i\in[r]\}\)

for some \(\tau\in S_\pi\). Moreover, the vertices added between adjacent gadget cells force any dominating set to select the corresponding component in a dominating set of size (2_r_-1)_k_<sup>2</sup>.

\(\triangleright\) Claim 18. (S_,k,n_) is a positive Grid Tiling instance if and only if \(G_\mathcal{S}^r\) is a positive (2_r_-1)_k_<sup>2</sup>-DS instance.

Then, for the bound on the radius-(2_r_-2) merge-width, the merge sequence is done similarly: first resolve all matchings and co-matchings inside gadget cells; then resolve the co-matchings and the matchings with the vertices between adjacent gadget cells; then add every remaining edge of \(G_\mathcal{S}^r\).

\(\triangleright\) Claim 19. \(\mathrm{mw}_{2r-2}(G_\mathcal{S}^r)=\mathcal{O}(r)\).

Using the same arguments as in Claim 17, it follows that for any functions _f(k_)=_o(k_) and _g(k_), solving _k_-Dominating Set on graphs with \(\mathrm{mw}_{f(k)}\le g(k)\) is W[1]-hard. \(\blacktriangleleft\)
